title: Subtract Until One Hits Zero
statement:
You have two non-negative integers a and b. One step subtracts the smaller number from the larger one and keeps the result in place of the larger. If they are equal, subtract either one from the other.

Repeat steps while both numbers are positive. Return how many steps happen before one of them becomes 0. If one of them is already 0, the answer is 0.

The numbers can be as large as 10⁹, so a step-by-step simulation is too slow in the worst case.

examples.why: Equal numbers: one subtraction makes one of them 0.
One number is already 0, so no step is taken.

hints: Simulate a few pairs by hand. When the smaller number stays the same for many steps in a row, what is happening?
While a ≥ b, you keep subtracting the same b from a. How many times can you subtract b from a before a drops below b?
That is a / b steps at once, leaving a % b. Then swap roles. This is Euclid's algorithm with a step counter.

explain.intuition:
Simulating one subtraction at a time is correct but can take a billion steps for (10⁹, 1). Notice that while a ≥ b, every step subtracts the same b from a. You subtract it exactly ⌊a / b⌋ times before a becomes smaller than b, and what remains is a % b.

So one division replaces a whole run of steps: add ⌊a / b⌋ to the count, replace a with a % b, and swap roles. This is exactly Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor, which needs only O(log min(a, b)) rounds. Equal numbers fit in naturally: ⌊a / a⌋ = 1 step, remainder 0.
steps: While a > 0 and b > 0: make sure a ≥ b by swapping if needed.
Add ⌊a / b⌋ to steps and set a = a % b.
pitfalls: Simulating one subtraction per loop iteration. (10⁹, 1) then takes 10⁹ iterations.
Counting Euclid rounds instead of adding the quotients. (7, 3) has two rounds but five steps.
Forgetting the zero cases: if either number starts at 0, the loop must not run at all.

solutions.title: Simulate every step
solutions.idea: Do exactly what the statement says, one subtraction per iteration.

solutions.title: Euclid with quotients
solutions.idea: A run of subtractions of the same number is one division. Add the quotient, keep the remainder, swap.

followups: Return the final non-zero number. What is it in terms of a and b?
How many rounds of the division loop can there be at most for numbers up to 10⁹? Which pairs are the worst case?
